title: High-Access Employees
statement:
Each entry `access_times[i] = [name, time]` records that the employee `name` used the system at `time`, a four-digit 24-hour clock reading such as `"0800"` or `"2250"`. All entries belong to one single day, and the same employee may appear many times (even at the same time; each entry is a separate access).

An employee is **high-access** when three or more of their accesses fall within one period of less than an hour: some three of their times differ pairwise by at most 59 minutes. Times exactly 60 minutes apart are not in the same period, and the day does not wrap around (`"2350"` and `"0005"` are 23 hours and 45 minutes apart).

Return the names of all high-access employees, each once, in any order.
constraints: access_times[i][0] contains only lowercase English letters
access_times[i][1] is a valid 24-hour time from "0000" to "2359"
notes:
## Intuition

The brute force checks, for every access, how many of that employee's accesses land in the hour starting there: O(n²). Sorting makes it simpler. Once one employee's times are in increasing order, any three times within an hour can be taken as three neighbours, so it is enough to compare each time with the one two places earlier. Sorting all entries by name first and then by time puts each employee's times side by side, so a single scan handles everyone.

## Approach

1. Turn each entry into `[name, minutes]`, where `minutes = hours * 60 + minutes past the hour`.
2. Sort `entries` by name, breaking ties by `minutes`.
3. For each `i` from 2, look at `entries[i - 2]`. If it has the same name and is less than 60 minutes earlier, the three entries `i - 2`, `i - 1`, `i` (all that employee's, by the sort) fit in one period.
4. Add the name to `result` unless it was the last name added; equal names are adjacent, so this avoids duplicates.

## Example 1, step by step

The minutes are `a: 349, 332, 381` and `b: 297, 340`. After sorting, `entries` is `[a,332], [a,349], [a,381], [b,297], [b,340]`.

- `i = 2`: `[a,381]` against `[a,332]`: same name, `381 - 332 = 49 < 60`, so `"a"` is added.
- `i = 3`: `[b,297]` against `[a,349]`: different names, skip.
- `i = 4`: `[b,340]` against `[a,381]`: different names, skip.

The answer is `["a"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scan is O(n).
- Space: O(n) for `entries`.

## Pitfalls

- The window is strict: a difference of exactly 60 minutes does not count, so test `< 60`.
- Compare times as minutes, not as four-digit numbers: `1000 - 0959` is 41 as numbers but only 1 minute.
- The clock does not wrap: `"2350"` and `"0005"` are far apart.
- Repeated identical entries are separate accesses, and a name must be reported only once.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `entries` | `[name, minutes]` pairs, sorted by name, then time |
| `i` | index of the third access of a candidate triple |
| `name`, `minutes` | the employee and time at `entries[i]` |
| `result` | high-access names found so far, each once |

narration.2: Convert every time to minutes since midnight so differences are real minute gaps.
narration.3: Sort by name, then by time, so each employee's accesses sit together in time order.
narration.6: Treat each entry from index 2 on as the last of three neighbouring accesses.
narration.8: Two places back belongs to someone else, so these are not three accesses by one employee.
narration.11: The three accesses span 60 minutes or more, so they do not share one period.
narration.14: Equal names are adjacent, so checking the last added name avoids duplicates.
narration.18: Every employee with three accesses inside an hour has been collected.
